Audience vs Community: What Actually Makes the Difference?

Analysislowob research

By lowob · 18 May 2026 · 8-minute read · Growth

A large follower count or Discord server is not automatically a community. The difference is whether people help, learn from and create value for one another. An audience receives. A customer transacts. A user engages with a product. A community member participates in a group whose value is partly created by other members. Each needs a different strategy, and the most common mistake is designing for one while measuring another.

This piece is the definitional starting point of our guide to building a community that lasts.

Many companies say they have a community because they have opened a Discord server, accumulated followers or issued a token. Those things can assemble people in the same digital space. They do not automatically create relationships, shared identity or participation.

Four groups companies routinely confuse

GroupWho they areWhere value flowsWhat to measure
AudiencePeople who pay attention to the company or its ideasCompany to individualQualified reach, return readership
Customers or usersPeople who exchange money, data or behaviour for a product outcome; they may never meetProduct to individualActivation, retention, revenue
Network participantsPeople whose activity increases the utility of a shared system: developers, liquidity providers, creators, node operatorsParticipant to systemIntegrations, liquidity, uptime, usage of what they built
CommunityPeople who develop repeated relationships, shared norms, identity and mutual value around an interest or purposeMember to memberPeer help, distinct contributors, returning members

One person can occupy several roles. A developer may use the product, contribute code, answer peer questions and publicly advocate for the network. But the roles should not be treated as identical.

Research on online communities draws a related line. Kraut and Resnick's Building Successful Online Communities (MIT Press) treats building members' commitment through the theory of interpersonal bond formation as a separate design problem from encouraging contribution. Bonds between people are what distinguish the last row of the table from the first three.

The peer-value test

Remove the company from the room for one week. Would members still help one another, exchange knowledge, build things, organise activities or maintain relationships?

If all activity stops, the company may have an audience or support channel rather than a community. That is not necessarily a failure. A useful customer-support environment can be more valuable than a forced community. The mistake is designing for one group while measuring another.

The test can be run on data as well as by absence. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities, a vendor study of its own customers, found that outside GitHub, community members replied to each other 28% of the time against 13% for company staff. Where members answer more questions than staff do, there is peer value. Where staff answer everything, the company is running a support desk with a chat interface.

If the only reason members return is to receive your announcements, you have a distribution channel, not a community.

Community requires a reason to return

People do not repeatedly participate because a brand wants engagement. They return because the group provides a recurring form of value.

Some communities bring together experts who exchange information and help one another solve problems. Others give members a professional identity, a chance to collaborate, influence over a product or access to economic opportunities. People may also return because they are learning, gaining recognition or developing a sense of belonging.

The company should be able to complete this sentence:

Members return because they can ______ with people they could not easily ______ elsewhere.

If the answer is "receive our announcements", the company has a distribution channel. Our piece on community management versus social media management sets out why those are different jobs needing different people.

Design participation, not just programming

Events, AMAs, office hours and announcements are programming. They can create occasions for participation, but only if members have a role beyond attendance.

Participation often starts with observing and asking questions. As people become more comfortable, they share useful resources, join working sessions and contribute to projects. Eventually some members lead discussions or shape a product or governance decision. Each stage needs a clear invitation, not just a request to "engage".

Expect the ladder to narrow. Jakob Nielsen's analysis of participation inequality found that in most online communities about 90% of people only read, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. Nielsen argued the pattern cannot be removed, only improved: lower the barrier to a first contribution, let people edit rather than create from scratch, and promote quality rather than volume. Each of those is an invitation to the next rung.

RungTypical behaviourThe invitation that moves people up
ObserveReads, attendsA starter resource and a clear first step
AskPosts a questionA fast, useful reply from a member or host
SharePosts a resource or answerPublic credit for the contribution
ContributeJoins a working session or projectA specific brief with an end date
LeadRuns a discussion or shapes a decisionA real decision, and evidence it was shaped

Measure relationships and contribution

Member count is the easiest number to inflate and one of the weakest indicators of community health.

Look at how many newcomers make a meaningful first contribution, how often people return and whether members help each other without relying on staff. Track distinct contributors, the time to a useful response, and work that generates product, support, knowledge or distribution value. These measures tell a more useful story than server size or message volume alone.

Discord's own Server Insights guidance treats engagement and retention as the main signs of health. It separates visitors, who open a channel, from communicators, who post, and tracks new member retention as the share of new members who return after a week. It also notes that engagement and retention are among the factors it reviews for its Partner programme.

The field still leans on headcount. CMX's 2025 survey of community professionals found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%, and only 24% could confidently put a financial value on their community. Our piece Community is a job, not a number sets out the contribution measures that fit each kind of community.

Be willing to say you do not need a community

Some products need excellent onboarding, support, education and customer communication, not a member-led social system.

Community becomes commercially useful when peer relationships, contribution, identity or network participation improve the product or purpose. If none of those conditions exists, forcing customers into a chat room creates operational cost without durable value. That cost is real: CMX found 17% of organisations had no one working full time on community, the highest share it had recorded. An under-resourced community that nobody needs is worse than none.

Where the honest answer is an audience, build an audience well; our piece on measuring brand in B2B covers how to judge one. Where the answer is users, invest in onboarding and retention. The strongest community strategy sometimes begins with intellectual honesty: deciding which group the company actually has and what that group needs.

lowob takeaways

  • Name the group you have. Distinguish audiences, customers, users, network participants and active contributors.
  • Run the peer-value test. If activity stops when the company steps away, it is an audience or support channel.
  • Create reasons for members to help one another. Complete the "members return because" sentence before building anything.
  • Measure participation and relationships. Peer help, distinct contributors and returning members, not member count.

Common questions

What is the difference between an audience and a community?

An audience receives from the company; value flows one way. A community is a group whose value is partly created by its members, through repeated relationships, shared norms and mutual help.

How do you know if you have a real community?

Run the peer-value test: remove the company for a week and see whether members still help each other, share knowledge and organise. Also compare how many questions members answer against how many staff answer.

What metrics show community health?

Newcomers' first meaningful contributions, return frequency, peer help without staff, distinct contributors, time to a useful response and work that creates product, support, knowledge or distribution value.

Does every company need a community?

No. Some products are better served by strong onboarding, support and education. A community is worth building when peer relationships or contribution improve the product or its purpose.

Sources and notes

  • Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights, undated. Platform documentation; definitions apply to Discord servers.
  • Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report, 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room; 2022 data.
  • Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule, 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
  • Kraut and Resnick, Building Successful Online Communities: Evidence-Based Social Design, MIT Press, paperback edition February 2016. Academic book; publisher description consulted.
  • CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report, 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals; CMX is owned by Bevy, a community software vendor; self-reported.
